fr:title.text: Theme Studio — the current forest theme

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Theme Studio — the current forest theme

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Reference for the theme currently shipping on this forest — the Theme Studio redesign (April 2026). Supersedes the earlier theming note Forest Theming Customization, which describes the upstream base theme plus a thin Dracula overlay and is no longer accurate. Background on why theming lives in a fork at all is in Forking Forester.

The theme is a git submodule at ~/forest/theme/, declared in .gitmodules. The submodule URL points to a personal fork — git@github.com:stschaef/forester-base-theme.git — not the upstream Sourcehut repo. The fork tracks upstream's 4.3.0 tag as its base, with Theme Studio commits layered on top.
Inside the submodule, the live remotes are:

html:ul.html:li: origin → https://git.sr.ht/~jonsterling/forester-base-theme (read-only upstream, for pulling new releases)
fork → git@github.com:stschaef/forester-base-theme.git (read/write, what the submodule actually checks out)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The forest repo records a commit SHA in the theme submodule; the build configs (forest.toml, public.toml) point Forester at theme/ for XSL templates and at theme/style.css, theme/forester.js, theme/forester-extras.js for the bundled assets. Forester copies these into output/ on each build.
Key files inside the submodule:

html:ul.html:li: style.css — ~930 lines, the entire Theme Studio palette (see theme architecture)
style.css.upstream-bak — preserved copy of the pre-redesign upstream CSS, kept for reference
forester-extras.js — the persistent left rail builder, kept separate so re-bundling forester.js from upstream sources doesn't clobber it
forester.js — bundled from javascript-source/forester.js via bundle-js.sh (esbuild)
tree.xsl, default.xsl, core.xsl, links.xsl, metadata.xsl — XSL pipeline, near-upstream
themes/dracula.css — legacy single-overlay file from before the redesign; superseded by inline theme blocks in style.css, kept around but no longer wired up
fonts/ — only KaTeX fonts; body/heading fonts now come from the system stack or web fonts loaded by name (Newsreader, Jost)

fr:title.text: Theme Studio architecture — six themes via token overrides

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Theme Studio architecture — six themes via token overrides

fr:mainmatter.html:p: style.css defines one set of base design tokens on :root (colors, fonts, spacing, taxon stamp palette, TODO state colors) and six themes that override those tokens. Each theme is dispatched by \meta{theme}{X}, which the XSL pipeline turns into article.theme-X; the override block lives on :root:has(article.theme-X) so the tokens flow through the whole document, not just the article.
The six themes:

html:ul.html:li: paper — Field Notes inspired; burnt orange · burgundy · slate blue · mustard on cream; Newsreader serif body, Jost display
dracula — refined dark; the original overlay, now folded into the unified file
academic — high-contrast scholarly light; Newsreader throughout, italic small-caps taxons
solarized — Ethan Schoonover's warm-neutral palette
editorial — Swiss / bold Helvetica with vermilion accent and heavy display sizes
blueprint — ice-on-navy dark variant with a faint grid backdrop on body

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Beyond the token block, each theme adds a small set of theme-internal flourishes via article.theme-X selectors — depth-cycled subtree border colors in paper, the grid background in blueprint, italic emphasis recolor in dracula, etc.
The default theme is paper, set as an XSL variable in tree.xsl:
When a tree omits \meta{theme}, the XSL falls back to this default; \meta{theme}{none} explicitly opts out (no theme class is emitted, base tokens win).

The sticky left sidebar — name (link to home), email, and the page TOC — is built at runtime by theme/forester-extras.js. The upstream theme's top nav bar is hidden via a display: none rule on header.header in style.css; the JS scrapes its Home link before removing it and rebuilds an <aside class="site-sidebar"> as the first child of grid-wrapper.

Identity values are hard-coded in the JS — currently Steven Schaefer and stschaef@umich.edu in the SITE constant at the top of the file. Editing those is the one place to change what the rail displays.
The rail also pulls the page TOC (navtoc) into itself when present, separated by an <hr class="site-div">. CSS in style.css sets up the grid:

Below 1000px the sidebar reverts to static flow above the article. forester-extras.js also strips the trailing period the XSL bakes onto stamped taxon and TODO-status labels (TODO., Reference.) — subtree numbers like 1. are left alone.
Because forester.js is rebundled from upstream sources via bundle-js.sh, the rail logic lives in its own file so upstream re-bundles don't clobber it. tree.xsl sources both scripts.
Theme dispatch is entirely in theme/tree.xsl, around lines 76–87. The XSL writes a class attribute on .tree-container computed from \meta{theme}{...}:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: <xsl:choose> <xsl:when test="...meta[@name='theme'] = 'none'" /> <xsl:when test="...meta[@name='theme']"> <xsl:text> theme-</xsl:text> <xsl:value-of select="...meta[@name='theme']" /> </xsl:when> <xsl:when test="$default-theme != ''"> <xsl:text> theme-</xsl:text> <xsl:value-of select="$default-theme" /> </xsl:when> </xsl:choose>
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Three cases:

html:ul.html:li: Tree sets \meta{theme}{X} → emits class="... theme-X", which activates the matching :root:has(article.theme-X) block in style.css
Tree sets \meta{theme}{none} → no theme class; base :root tokens win (academic-light fallback)
No theme meta → falls through to $default-theme (currently paper)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: To add a new theme, the workflow is: pick a name, add a :root:has(article.theme-<name>) { ... } block in style.css overriding the relevant tokens, and optionally a few article.theme-<name> selectors for theme-specific structural touches. No XSL or compiler change needed.
To change the site-wide default, edit the $default-theme variable at the top of tree.xsl.

The XSL still emits layout-X classes on both grid-wrapper and .tree-container when a tree sets \meta{layout}{X} (see tree.xsl:63-75), but the Theme Studio style.css has zero .layout-* rules. So \meta{layout}{wide}, dashboard, table, kanban all attach a class that styles nothing.

The upstream-backup CSS (theme/style.css.upstream-bak) had twelve .layout-* rules covering layout-wide, layout-table, layout-kanban. None of them survived the Theme Studio rewrite. layout-dashboard was never styled even in the upstream version — the dashboard layout described in the forest CLAUDE.md was aspirational.
Trees that still set \meta{layout}{wide} (the index, dashboard, a few public refs) render exactly as if the meta were absent. Either:

html:ul.html:li: Port the relevant rules out of style.css.upstream-bak into style.css, or
Strip the now-meaningless \meta{layout} declarations from the trees that set them

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The CLAUDE.md doc still lists \meta{layout}{wide|dashboard|table|kanban} as a supported customization surface; that section needs updating in lockstep with whichever fix lands.
Editing the theme means editing the submodule. The flow:

html:ul.html:li: Edit style.css, forester-extras.js, or whichever file
git commit inside theme/ (the commit lands on the fork remote's branch)
git push fork to publish
Back in ~/forest: git add theme then git commit to bump the recorded submodule SHA

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Forgetting the second commit means the forest repo still points at the old theme SHA — locally everything looks right, but other clones (and forest-pull.service on the home server) will check out the stale version.
For local iteration, ./server.sh runs Forester in dev mode with fswatch on both trees/ and theme/; CSS edits hot-rebuild without touching git at all. Only commit when the change is settled.
To pull in upstream Forester theme releases:

html:ul.html:li: Inside theme/: git fetch origin
git merge <upstream-tag> or rebase the Theme Studio commits onto the new tag
Expect conflicts in style.css and tree.xsl — these are the most heavily modified files
forester-extras.js should never conflict (upstream doesn't know about it)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The whole subsystem assumes you also have read access to ~/ocaml-forester for reference — when an XSL change behaves unexpectedly, the upstream compiler source (lib/frontend/Htmx_client.ml, lib/parser/) is the authoritative explanation of what classes and attributes the pipeline emits.

Deprecated (2026-05-29). This investigation predates the Theme Studio redesign — most concrete claims here (single Dracula overlay, Inria Sans bundled fonts, \meta{layout}{wide} actually working) are no longer true. See Theme Studio — the current forest theme for the current architecture. Kept for historical context.

Investigation note: how much of the forest's look — fonts, layout, home page, color — can I customize without forking the compiler? Inspired by Matteo Capucci's forest, whose home page and overall typography depart noticeably from the default Forester theme.

The current theme is the upstream Forester base theme plus a few local additions — see theme/style.css (~830 lines), the Dracula theme overlay at theme/themes/dracula.css, the bundled Inria Sans @font-face declarations, and the dashboard's grid/column layout driven by \meta{layout}{wide}. The XSL pipeline (default.xsl → core.xsl, tree.xsl, links.xsl, metadata.xsl) is unchanged from upstream.
In rough order of cost to change, these are the levers Forester actually exposes.

Anything visual — fonts, colors, spacing, max-widths, column behavior, sticky sidebars, link styling, code block treatment — is a theme/style.css edit. A new theme like themes/dracula.css demonstrates the pattern: scope rules under a class injected by \meta{theme}{name} so multiple themes can coexist. Capucci's narrower main column, prominent serif body, and quiet metadata are almost certainly all CSS.

Add .woff2 files under theme/fonts/ and declare them via @font-face in style.css, then update the body font-family stack. Replacing Inria Sans with a serif (e.g. EB Garamond, Crimson Pro, Equity, Concourse) or a more distinctive sans (Inter Display, Fraunces) is a one-file edit. KaTeX fonts are independent and should be left alone.

\meta{layout}{wide|dashboard|table|kanban} and \meta{theme}{dracula|...} inject CSS classes (see the compiler's Htmx_client.ml) that you can target from style.css. New layouts cost nothing on the OCaml side — pick a name, add the class hook, write the CSS. The home page already exploits this with layout-wide.

The home page is just a tree (trees/public/index.tree) — its structure is fully under your control via \transclude, \grid/\col, and per-tree metadata. Capucci-style "front of forest" layouts (a short bio, a hand-curated featured-trees list, a recent-activity column) are achievable today by editing index.tree and writing a couple of CSS rules; no compiler change needed.

Structural changes — moving the TOC, suppressing metadata blocks, restructuring the article header, changing how transclusions are wrapped — live in theme/tree.xsl (~490 lines) and friends. Editable in-place, but easy to break, and changes drift from upstream on every theme/ submodule update. Reserve for things CSS genuinely cannot do.

Behavioral changes — collapsible sections, hover transclusions, search affordances — go here. Highest blast radius and least likely to survive an upstream update; consider only after CSS and XSL have been ruled out.

New CSS class injection points, new metadata-driven hooks, new built-in macros, new Datalog relations. Already on the table via the forkester effort; should remain a last resort for theming work specifically.

html:ul.html:li: Narrower body column with a serif. A 60–70ch max-width on the article column, paired with a serif body font, is the single biggest visual shift and is pure CSS.
Quieter metadata. Default Forester surfaces tree IDs, dates, taxons fairly prominently; Capucci tucks them away. .metadata { font-size: 0.85em; color: var(--muted) } territory.
Restructured home page. Replace the current bio + transclusion stack with a hand-curated front matter (recent writing, ongoing projects, a "what I'm reading" block) — pure index.tree edit.
Sectioned sidebar nav. A persistent left rail listing top-level topics. Achievable with a new \meta{layout}{...} that adds a sidebar slot, then CSS grid for placement.
Should new themes be shipped as switchable overlays (\meta{theme}{name}, like Dracula today) or as a single replaced base style? Overlays let you A/B variants per tree but balloon CSS quickly.
How much should diverge from the upstream base theme before maintenance pain (submodule conflicts on theme/) outweighs the visual gain? Vendoring theme/ fully is one answer.
Do any of the desired layout changes actually require XSL edits, or is CSS grid + class hooks sufficient? Worth prototyping the Capucci home-page rework in pure CSS first to find out.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pick one Capucci-inspired change — most likely the narrow-serif body — and prototype it as a new \meta{theme}{...} overlay so it can coexist with the current look. That single experiment will surface most of the customization-cost questions above without committing to a full redesign.

For nearly the past year I have stopped using Forester. I initially found it quite compelling, but it was not capable of sufficiently encapsulating a broad set of features that lower my cognitive load enough for it to fully integrate into my thought patterns.

Org Roam, on the other hand, is easy to use and has a richer set of "tooling", for lack of a better word, atop it. For instance, management of org agenda, todo lists, and emacs support. I had used org mode more intensively before my switch to Forester, and I've recently found myself returning to it. Despite the niceties of org mode, I would much rather use Forester. Datalog is quite nice for creating custom queries, transclusion is wonderful, there is a glorious rendered version that can also double as a personal website.

I hope none of these thoughts come across as distaste for Forester. It truly is wonderful, but it is not yet the well-oiled fix that is uniquely tailored to satiate my individual needs. I think its unreasonable to expect anything off the shelf to be a magic fix. Over the past year, I've had many thoughts on what I'd like out of a tool like org or Forester, and I've just let these thoughts sit. I hardly have time to do my job, let alone morph Forester into my own personal digital brain.

I think I would also lack the stamina to coordinate with Jon and Kento in properly contributing. Perhaps this is just laziness from me, but I really don't have it in me to make this sort of customization feel like a job. Of course, I don't want to deliberately write bad code. Primarily, I don't want things like my nix, emacs, or Forester configurations to be beholden to external stakeholders. Further, I feel that enough of Forester is liable to be changed that I have been reluctant to lean into things like custom theming or hacking the compiler in a way that might not be easily accepted as a patch.

In tandem with other vibecoding experiments lately (which I should write about separately; TLDR, they have often been unexpectedly successful), I have decided that I simply won't care about trying to develop these changes to Forester person. Rather, I am simply aiming to specify behaviors. If the tool does what I need it to, I am not going to argue with the machine. Bad is good or something like that.

So my tentative plan is to let Claude extend Forester as I need, and I will deliberately aim to not think of the code directly. Instead, I am treating Forester like a black box tool that let's me manage my thoughts and interactions with my machine in a low-friction way. I'm willing to lets the code be AI slop so long as it continues to aid me toward this end.

I have begun this journey today and I now have Dracula theming, wide layouts, a collapsible table of contents, multicolumn, a TODO system, configured the edit button in dev mode to open emacs instead of VSCode, captured much of the functionality of Org roam, and keybinds that let me use these new Roam-like commands in a low effort manner in Emacs. This was all in a single day of me multitasking and using natural language to instruct Claude to write this. I know there is a lot of AI haters out there, but its ridiculous to blindly be a Luddite.

Sure there are reasons to dislike AI: overvaluation that will surely devastate the economy when it comes crashing down, environmental worries, IP concerns, job insecurity, virtue signalling to all your FOSS homies, and much more. Those all still remain true, but none invalidate the utility of giving myself a tool that will allow me to keep my head on straight. That is, the forest/Forester as I need it, not the coding model. Maybe its just the ADHD speaking, but I find these sorts of aides in lower cognitive burden invaluable. There is not enough self-denial and ideological purism in me to refuse access to such help. In many ways, this is one of the beauties of having tools and machines in the first place.

I should likely message the Forester mailing list about the sorts of features I create here. In such a message, I will be abundantly clear on the AI nature of the code and ask if they think it appropriate to share patches. I expect a polite decline, but I think its at least worth mentioning.
